blocks.text: The testis should have reached the deep inguinal ring by 5 months of gestation. Descent of testis: The developing testis is located in the upper abdomen, medial to the mesonephros during early intrauterine life, The processus vaginalis (peritoneal fold), extends in front of the testis toward the scrotum. Gubernaculum testis, a fibromuscular band, forms, connecting the mesonephric duct and the lower pole of the testis to the scrotum.
The descent of the testis is driven by differential growth in the embryo, beginning in the 2nd month of intrauterine life.
The normal timeline of testicular descent:

items.text: 2nd month of gestation: The testis starts its descent from the posterior abdominal wall.
3rd month of gestation: The testis reaches the iliac fossa. (Option B)
4th to 6th month of gestation: The testis descends further and rests at the deep inguinal ring during this period.
7th month of gestation: The testis traverses the inguinal canal. (Option D)
8th month of gestation: The testis reaches the superficial inguinal ring. (Option A)
9th month of gestation: The testis enters the scrotum At or just after birth: reaches the base of the scrotum.

The infracolic compartment is divided into right and left parts by the mesentery, not the falciform ligament.
**Peritoneal Cavity Peritoneal cavity is divided into two parts (Option A ruled out):** Abdominal cavity Pelvic cavity
Abdominal Cavity Divisions: Divided by the transverse colon and transverse mesocolon into:

items.text: Supracolic Compartment: Subdivided into subphrenic spaces by peritoneal reflection around the liver. (Option B ruled out)
Infracolic Compartment: Subdivided into right and left parts by the mesentery.
Paracolic Gutters:
Right Paracolic Gutter: Lateral side of the ascending colon. (Option D ruled out)
Left Paracolic Gutter: Lateral side of the descending colon.

blocks.text: Pelvic Cavity divisions: True Pelvis (Lesser Pelvis): The lower part that lies below the pelvic brim and contains the pelvic organs. Contents: Urinary bladder Reproductive organs (e.g., uterus, ovaries in females; prostate, seminal vesicles in males) Rectum and anal canal
False Pelvis (Greater Pelvis): The upper part, technically part of the abdominal cavity but supports the intestines and provides some protection to pelvic organs.

Epididymis is the structure where sperm mature and are stored but is not part of the spermatic cord; it is located on the surface of the testis. The spermatic cord is a collection of structures that pass to and fro from the testis through the inguinal canal. It extends from the deep inguinal ring to the posterior border of the testis and is covered by three fascial layers.
Contents of the spermatic cord:

items.text: Ductus deferens, in the posterior part (Option A)
Three arteries: Testicular artery, from abdominal aorta (Option B) Cremasteric artery, from the inferior epigastric artery.

blocks.text: **Artery to ductus deferens, from inferior vesical artery The pampiniform venous plexus (Option D):** Lymphatics, especially from testis draining into pre- and para-aortic nodes, and some from the coverings draining into external iliac nodes. Nerves: Genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve, and sympathetic fibers accompany the arteries. Remains of processus vaginalis Fig: Transverse section of the spermatic cord
The most superficial layer is the skin. Deep to the skin is the superficial fascia, which has two layers.

items.text: a. Camper fascia is called a fatty layer of subcutaneous tissue.
b. Scarpa fascia is called the membranous layer of subcutaneous tissue.

items.text: a. External oblique muscle.

Below the arcuate line, the posterior layer of the rectus sheath is absent, leaving the rectus abdominis muscle in direct contact with the transversalis fascia.
Fig: Rectus sheath at different levels
The formation of rectus sheath differs from the above downward as follows:

items.text: 1. Above the level of costal margin: The anterior wall is formed by the aponeurosis of the external oblique only. The posterior wall is deficient and muscle lies directly on the 5th, 6th, and 7th costal cartilage.

2. Between costal margin and arcuate line: Anterior wall is formed by the fusion of aponeurosis of external oblique with the anterior lamina of aponeurosis of internal oblique. The posterior wall is formed by the fusion of aponeurosis of the transversus abdominis with the posterior lamina of the aponeurosis of the internal oblique.

3. Below the level of the arcuate line: The anterior wall is formed by the aponeuroses of all three flat muscles (the aponeuroses of transversus abdominis and internal oblique are fused but the aponeurosis of external oblique remains separate). The posterior wall is deficient.

blocks.text: **At the level of the xiphoid process (Option A):** Above this level, the rectus sheath is made up of both the anterior and posterior layers formed by the aponeuroses of the abdominal muscles.
**At the level of the umbilicus (Option B):** Here, the rectus sheath still has anterior and posterior layers, but the arrangement starts to change as you move downward.

The roof of the inguinal canal is formed by the arching fibers of the internal oblique and the transversus abdominis muscles, not the external oblique aponeurosis. The inguinal canal is a passageway in the lower abdominal wall.
Contents of inguinal canal: In males: Spermatic cord and ilioinguinal nerve (Options B and D) In females: Round ligament of the uterus and ilioinguinal nerve (Option B)
The boundaries of the inguinal canal are:
Anterior wall: It is formed from superficial to deep by: Skin Superficial fascia in the whole extent. External oblique aponeurosis Internal oblique muscle fibers, in lateral one-third.

Posterior wall: It is formed from deep to superficial by: Fascia transversalis, in the whole extent (Option A) Conjoint tendon, in medial two-third Reflected part of the inguinal ligament, in the medial-most part.
Roof: It is formed by the lower arched fibers of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles.
Floor: It is formed by: Grooved upper surface of the inguinal ligament in the whole extent Abdominal surface of the lacunar ligament at the medial end.
The inguinal canal runs between these structures, with the inguinal ligament forming the inferior boundary and the iliopsoas muscle lying posterior. Relations of the inguinal canal:

rows: Has a defect called the deep inguinal ring, through which the testes and spermatic cord pass. Site for indirect inguinal hernias. Anterior to parietal peritoneum. Forms the posterior in the whole extent. (Option A)
Formed by the inferior epigastric vessels.
Remnant of the urachus (from the allantois).
Remnant of the obliterated umbilical artery.
Small muscle attaching to the pubic bone. Rectus abdominis lies above it. Covered by the rectus sheath and supplied by the subcostal nerve (T12).
Does not form the anterior wall of the inguinal canal. Contributes to the roof and posterior wall. Combines with internal oblique to form the conjoint tendon.
Forms parts of the anterior, roof, and posterior walls of the inguinal canal. Contributes to cremasteric muscle and fascia.
Aponeurosis forms the anterior wall of the inguinal canal and the superficial inguinal ring. Forms external spermatic fascia.

blocks.text: The inguinal canal does not contain the inferior epigastric vessels. The vessels are located medial to the deep inguinal ring, and the canal contains structures such as the spermatic cord (in males) or the round ligament (in females). (Option B)
The deep inguinal ring is located lateral (not medial) to the inferior epigastric vessels. (Option C)
The floor of the inguinal canal is not formed by the conjoint tendon. The floor is primarily formed by the inguinal ligament. (Option D)

The femoral triangle is an important anatomical region in the upper thigh, where key neurovascular structures pass, and it's clinically relevant for procedures like catheterization and palpating the femoral pulse. The lateral boundary of the femoral triangle is formed by the sartorius muscle. The iliacus and psoas major muscles form a part of the floor of the femoral triangle, not its lateral boundary.
Femoral Triangle Boundaries Contents

items.text: Lateral Boundary: Medial margin of the sartorius muscle.
Medial Boundary: Medial margin of the adductor longus muscle.
Apex: The point where the sartorius overlaps the adductor longus.
Floor: Laterally: Iliacus and psoas major muscles. Medially: Pectineus and adductor longus muscles.
Roof: Formed by the overlying fascia lata.

blocks.text: The structures are arranged from medial to lateral in the following order (VAN): Femoral vein (most medial) and Its Tributaries Femoral artery and Its Branches Femoral nerve (most lateral)

Femoral Sheath Nerves: Femoral Nerve Nerve to Pectineus Femoral Branch of Genitofemoral Nerve Lateral Cutaneous Nerve of the Thigh Deep Inguinal Lymph Nodes Femoral Ring- Base (upper end) of Femoral Canal Boundaries Contents Anterior: Inguinal ligament Posterior: Pectineus and its covering fascia Medial: Concave margin of lacunar ligament Lateral: Femoral vein Lymph node of Cloquet (Rosenmüller) Lymphatics Areolar tissue
The femoral ring, surrounded by the inguinal ligament, lacunar ligament, pectineal ligament, and femoral vein, creates a narrow space.
This makes femoral hernias highly prone to strangulation, as the herniated tissue can easily get trapped, leading to compromised blood supply and potential ischemia.
The rotation of the stomach and duodenum incorporates the upper right part of the peritoneal cavity into the lesser sac.
In the given image,

items.text: a- epiploic foramen
b- lesser sac
c- greater sac
d- greater omentum

blocks.text: Formation of the Lesser Sac
The growth of the right lobe of the liver pulls the ventral mesentery to the right, causing the rotation of the stomach and duodenum.

This rotation incorporates the upper right part of the peritoneal cavity into the lesser sac. The right border of the ventral mesentery becomes the right border of the lesser omentum and forms the anterior boundary of the entrance into the lesser sac.
Formation of the Greater Sac
The remaining part of the peritoneal cavity, not included in the lesser sac, is called the greater sac. (Option C ruled out)
The greater sac and lesser sac communicate through the epiploic foramen. (Option A ruled out)
Formation of the Greater Omentum
The spleen develops in the upper part of the dorsal mesentery, and the greater omentum forms from the rapid growth of the dorsal mesentery below the spleen. (Option D ruled out)
Initially, the greater omentum extends from the greater curvature of the stomach to the posterior abdominal wall above the transverse mesocolon.

As it continues to grow, the greater omentum descends as an apron-like double layer of peritoneum in front of the transverse colon. Later, the posterior layer of the greater omentum fuses with the transverse mesocolon, attaching it to the anterior surface of the transverse colon. Over time, the greater omentum becomes fat-laden, and the inferior recess of the lesser sac extends between its layers.

The Pringle maneuver involves clamping the hepatoduodenal ligament, which contains the portal triad, to control bleeding in the liver or surrounding structures. This maneuver is performed at the epiploic foramen (Foramen of Winslow). The caudate lobe of the liver forms the superior boundary of the Epiploic Foramen.

Epiploic Foramen / Omental Foramen / Foramen of Winslow: A vertical slit-like opening connecting the lesser sac with the greater sac, located behind the right free margin of the lesser omentum at the level of the 12th thoracic vertebra.
Boundaries:

items.text: Anterior: Right free margin of the lesser omentum (portal vein, proper hepatic artery, bile duct) (Option D ruled out)
Posterior: Inferior vena cava, right suprarenal gland, T12 vertebra (Option A ruled out)
Superior: Caudate process of the liver
Inferior: First part of the duodenum, horizontal part of the hepatic artery (Option C ruled out)

blocks.text: Clinical Relevance: Pringle Maneuver: A technique to control bleeding from the liver by compressing the free edge of the lesser omentum.
Fluid Collections: The apposed walls of the foramen can lead to isolated fluid collections in the greater sac or omental bursa.

Pus moves from the lesser sac through the foramen of Winslow into the greater sac, enters the hepatorenal pouch of Morrison, continues through the paracolic gutter, then reaches the rectouterine pouch of Douglas, where a pelvic abscess may form.
Peritoneal Spaces

items.text: **Greater Sac:** Largest compartment of the peritoneal cavity, spanning the entire abdomen.
**Lesser Sac:** Smaller compartment, located behind the stomach, liver, and lesser omentum, as a diverticulum from the greater sac. Both the sacs can be connected through the foramen of Winslow.

blocks.text: Paracolic Gutters

items.text: **Right Paracolic Gutter:** Located lateral to the ascending colon, continuous with the hepatorenal pouch (Morrison’s pouch) above and pelvic cavity below. Infections may spread from the appendix or hepatorenal pouch.

**Left Paracolic Gutter:** Located lateral to the descending colon, limited by the phrenicocolic ligament above, and continuous with the pelvic cavity below. Infections may spread upward from the pelvis.

blocks.text: Subphrenic Spaces
Six spaces near the liver, important for surgeons due to frequent pus collection (subphrenic abscesses).

items.text: **Right side:**
Right posterior intraperitoneal compartment (Hepatorenal pouch or Morrison's pouch).
Right anterior intraperitoneal compartment.
Right extraperitoneal compartment.
**Left side:**
Left posterior intraperitoneal compartment.
Left anterior intraperitoneal compartment.
Left extraperitoneal compartment.

blocks.text: **Hepatorenal Pouch (Morison’s Pouch):** Located between the liver and right kidney, communicates with the lesser sac through the epiploic foramen. Most dependent part in the supine position, often collecting pus after upper abdominal surgery (e.g., cholecystectomy). Communicates with the rectouterine pouch via the right paracolic gutter, serving as a route for infection from the abdomen to the pelvis.
Pulmonary veins do not serve as a collateral pathway in cases of IVC obstruction.
**Vertebral venous plexus (Option A):** True statement, the vertebral venous plexus is a common collateral pathway for venous return in cases of IVC obstruction.

**Internal thoracic veins (Option B):** True statement, the internal thoracic veins (also called the internal mammary veins) are another common collateral route during IVC obstruction. They connect to the subclavian veins and can provide an alternative route for venous return to the heart.

**Superficial veins of the anterior abdominal wall (Option C):** True statement, the superficial veins of the anterior abdominal wall, particularly the paraumbilical veins, form collateral pathways through the epigastric veins. In the case of IVC obstruction, these veins become prominent and can provide venous drainage.
Inferior vena cava obstruction
Collaterals develop due to obstruction of the inferior vena cava.
Etiology:

items.text: Thrombosis
Embolism
Extrinsic compression like tumor, pregnancy

blocks.text: **Pathology:** Ultimately blood is connected to the superior vena cava through extensive venous collateral systems.
**Collateral systems:** Azygos–hemiazygos venous system, vertebral venous plexuses.
Superficial veins of the thoracic and abdominal walls- thoraco-epigastric anastomosis.
Note: Lumbar veins contribute significantly to these pathways.
Lumbar veins

**Thoraco-epigastric collateral:** The superior epigastric vein forms anastomose with lateral thoracic vein and the inferior epigastric vein forms anastomose with internal thoracic vein. The anastomosis formed is known as thoraco-epigastric anastomosis.

Lateral thoracic vein drains into the axillary vein. The axillary vein continues as the subclavian vein. The subclavian vein receives the internal thoracic vein. The subclavian vein drains into the brachiocephalic vein. Brachiocephalic vein drains into superior vena cava. Superior vena cava drains into the right atrium.

There are typically 4 Houston's valves in the human rectum. Houston's valves (or permanent folds) are semilunar (crescentic) transverse folds in the rectum. They are located against the concavities of the lateral curvatures of the rectum. They are formed by the reduplication of the mucous membrane containing submucous tissue and thickening of circular smooth muscle of the rectal wall.
Houston's valves are permanent and become more prominent when the rectum is distended. According to Houston, there are four valves numbered from above downward:

items.text: **First valve:** Located near the upper end, close to the rectosigmoid junction, projecting from the right or left wall.
**Second valve:** About 1 inch (2.5 cm) above the third fold, projecting from the left rectal wall along the concavity of the upper lateral curvature.

**Third valve:** The largest, most constant, and most important valve, located on the anterior and right wall of the rectum along the concavity of the middle lateral curvature, at the level of the upper end of the ampulla.
**Fourth valve:** Located on the left wall of the rectum along the concavity of the lower lateral curvature, about 2.5 cm below the third valve.

blocks.text: Marginal Artery of Drummond is a circumferential anastomotic arterial channel. It extends from the ileocaecal junction to the rectosigmoid junction. It is located approximately 3 cm from the inner margin of the colon. It is formed by the anastomoses between:

items.text: Colic branches of the superior mesenteric artery (i.e., ileocolic, right colic, and middle colic).
Colic branches of the inferior mesenteric artery (i.e., left colic and sigmoidal).

blocks.text: The vasa recta (small vessels) arise from the Marginal Artery of Drummond and supply the colon.

**Critical point of the colon:** It is located at the splenic flexure. At this level, the ascending branch of the left colic artery may fail to anastomose with the left branch of the middle colic artery. However, an anastomotic channel called the " arc of Riolan " exists between:

items.text: The main trunk of the middle colic artery.
The ascending branch of the left colic artery.

blocks.text: If the arc of Riolan is poorly developed, the arterial supply to the splenic flexure is compromised. As a result, the splenic flexure may undergo ischemic changes.

Plicae circulares are large, prominent circular folds found in the jejunum. They are designed to increase surface area for nutrient absorption. In contrast, the ileum has smaller, less prominent folds, and the duodenum has fewer plicae circulares. Plicae circulares are circular folds of the mucous membrane found in the

small intestine, particularly in the jejunum. These folds are more prominent, closely set, and contribute to the thicker feel of the jejunum when compared to the ileum, which has less prominent and more sparsely arranged folds. The plicae circulares increase the surface area, are more numerous in the jejunum, where the diameter of the intestine is slightly wider.
In contrast, the ileum contains many more aggregated lymph follicles (Peyer's patches) but fewer plicae circulares.
Differences between the Jejunum and the Ileum:

rows: Small, circular, and few in number, found only in the distal part of the jejunum
Large, oval, more in number, found throughout the ileum, maximum in the distal part
Contains less fat, becomes semitranslucent between the vasa recta, called peritoneal windows
Contains more fat, no peritoneal windows between the vasa recta
One or two rows with long vasa recta
Four or five rows with short vasa recta

blocks.text: The paraduodenal recess is an anatomical feature located to the left of the fourth part of the duodenum. It is situated behind the paraduodenal fold of the peritoneum. The key feature of this recess is that it contains the inferior mesenteric vein (IMV) in the free border of the paraduodenal fold.

**Duodenal Recesses:** At the duodenojejunal junction, small pocket-like pouches of peritoneum, called duodenal recesses, may occur. These recesses can sometimes lead to strangulated retroperitoneal hernias.
The key recesses around the duodenojejunal flexure are:

items.text: **Superior Duodenal Recess:** Located to the left of the upper end of the fourth part of the duodenum, behind the superior duodenojejunal fold, with its orifice facing downward.
**Inferior Duodenal Recess:** Found just below the superior recess, behind the inferior duodenojejunal fold, with its orifice facing upward.

**Paraduodenal Recess:** The lowest recess, located to the left of the fourth part of the duodenum behind the paraduodenal fold, with its orifice facing medially. The fold contains the inferior mesenteric vein.
**Retroduodenal Recess:** The largest, but rarely present; located behind the third and fourth parts of the duodenum, with its orifice facing downward and left.

blocks.text: The given image represents the mesentery. The attached border, or the root of mesentery, is attached to an oblique line across the posterior abdominal wall, extending from the duodenojejunal flexure to the ileocecal junction. The mesentery presents two borders:

items.text: **Attached border (or root).**
**Free border (or intestinal border).**

blocks.text: **Root of mesentery (attached border):** Extends from the duodenojejunal flexure to the ileocecal junction.
**Structures crossed by root of mesentery:**

**Free border (intestinal border):** Its length permits the free mobility of the loops of jejunum and ileum in the abdominal cavity. Near the intestinal border it presents fat-free oval/circular windows (translucent area) of peritoneum. The amount of fat is greater in the distal part of the mesentery.
The contents of the mesentery are:

items.text: Superior mesenteric artery and vein (in the root)—with vein being to the right of the artery.
Jejunal and ileal branches of superior mesenteric artery and accompanying veins.
Lymphatics (lacteals).
Lymph nodes (100–200 in number).
Autonomic nerve plexuses.
Fat and connective tissues.
Jejunum and ileum (enclosed in the free border).
